query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges primarily due to the thermally activated development of short‐range order at grain boundaries rather than from conventional precipitation. This ordering reduces grain-boundary cohesion under service-like thermal and mechanical loads, leading to toughness degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with complex composition and minimal preexisting grain-boundary ordering.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging with controlled cooling rate adjustments, where slower cooling promotes the development of short-range ordering at the grain boundaries and faster cooling suppresses it.
generation.conditions: Exposures to service-relevant temperatures (e.g., moderate to high temperatures that mimic operational environments) combined with mechanical loading regimes (e.g., tensile and creep tests) to simulate in-service stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary short-range order (SRO) evolving during thermal aging.
generation.mechanism: Under thermal and mechanical stress, slower cooling and prolonged aging allow local chemical ordering at grain boundaries to develop. This ordering lowers grain boundary cohesion, promoting intergranular crack initiation and propagation, which manifests as brittle behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy specimens subjected to slow cooling and extended aging will exhibit enhanced SRO at grain boundaries detectable via high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM or atom probe tomography) and concurrently show reduced ductility and lower fracture toughness compared to specimens quenched rapidly from solution heat treatment.
generation.baseline: The as-processed alloy state achieved via rapid cooling, which minimizes the development of SRO and exhibits higher toughness and ductility.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within service and loading conditions typical of high-temperature operational environments where oxidation and conventional precipitation are suppressed, and where mechanical loading (tensile/creep) is representative of engineering service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the degree of short-range ordering and the extent of toughness degradation is not fully established, and optimal aging conditions for pronounced SRO formation need further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens: one set is rapidly quenched after solution heat treatment (minimizing SRO development) and the other is subjected to slow controlled cooling followed by thermal aging to promote SRO. Both sets are then subjected to identical tensile and creep tests under service-relevant temperatures. Post-mortem high-resolution microscopy (TEM/atom probe) is used to quantify the degree of grain-boundary ordering.
measurements: Grain-boundary composition and ordering via TEM/atom probe analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically aged specimens (with slow cooling) do not show a statistically significant increase in short-range order at grain boundaries nor a corresponding decrease in toughness (relative to the quenched specimens), then the hypothesis that grain-boundary short-range ordering governs the emergence of brittle behavior in these alloys will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We used transmission electron microscope (TEM) to investigate the deformation mechanism of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs. The as‐printed samples exhibited the Kurdjumov–Sachs relationship between the FCC and BCC phases at their interface (Figure 4a). In contrast to conventionally fabricated EHEAs where the BCC lamellae consist of an ordered B2 with disordered BCC nanoprecipitates,[  ] the EHEAs exhibit a disordered BCC matrix with ordered B2 nanoprecipitates (Figure S5, Supporting Information). In conventional fabrication methods, such as casting, elemental diffusion occurs relatively freely during solidification due to lower cooling rates. This allows sufficient time for the formation of equilibrium ordered B2 phase as the matrix, accompanied by the precipitation of disordered BCC phase. In contrast, the ultra‐high cooling rates characteristic of LPBF processes (10⁶–10⁸ K s−1) significantly suppress atomic diffusion. Under these conditions, rapid solidification can shift the phase formation mechanism toward diffusion‐limited solidification, drastically restricting elemental partitioning and chemical ordering.[  ] Consequently, the resulting matrix tends to form a disordered BCC matrix d

During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

The effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties has been investigated for a high-entropy alloy (Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%)) fabricated by selective laser melting, the followings are findings of this work: Serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. The inferior ductility of straight grain boundary at 650°C was attributed to the grain boundary embrittlement caused by strain concentration at triple junctions and fast intergranular crack propagation. The slow cooling process of the post heat treatment could coarsen the γ′ particles and encourage interactions with mobile grain boundaries to from serrated grain boundaries. Analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. Serrated grain boundaries could reduce local strain concentration and provide resistance against intergranular cracking.

frame.system: A compositionally complex, initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy engineered for demanding service conditions.
frame.goal: To identify and test a mechanistic hypothesis that explains the emergence of brittle behavior (toughness degradation) in such high-entropy alloys, distinguishing its behavior from that of conventional alloys.
frame.limitation: Although these alloys suppress conventional degradation mechanisms (rapid grain coarsening, deleterious intermetallic formation), it is not established what governs toughness degradation in the absence of the typical grain-boundary segregation and precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
constraints: the alloy must remain compositionally complex
be suitable for demanding engineering service
frame.regime: Testing should span conditions that mimic service boundaries, including environments of high temperature (to probe softening mechanisms) and low temperature (to assess embrittlement), combined with mechanical loading regimes that represent operational stress states.
prior_attempts: Conventional alloy studies focused on grain-boundary segregation and precipitation as causes for brittleness; these mechanisms are suppressed in high-entropy alloys. Thus, traditional explanations and testing regimes do not capture the distinct behavior observed in high-entropy systems.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on high-entropy alloys have largely focused on understanding deformation through dislocation mechanisms and on engineering the grain boundary morphology—in one work, modifying the boundary from straight to serrated reduced intergranular fracture and hot ductility drop. Other studies have shown that conventional deleterious effects such as grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation are suppressed in HEAs, but subtle changes in grain-boundary chemistry or local short‐range order can still influence mechanical performance. In some refractory and medium‐entropy systems, thermal treatments have led to changes in the local composition (or chemical short‐range ordering) that correlate with embrittlement or softening upon aging. However, a mechanism explaining a toughness degradation in an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex alloy, distinct from conventional precipitation-driven embrittlement, remains incomplete.
decision.unsolved: It remains unestablished whether brittle behavior in these HEAs is governed by an evolution of local chemical ordering at the grain boundaries under service conditions rather than by conventional grain-boundary segregation and precipitation. In other words, the link between thermal/mechanical exposure and the emergence of subtle local compositional fluctuations (or short-range order) that lower grain-boundary cohesion in a single-phase HEA has not been decisively elucidated.
decision.lever: Thermal aging with controlled cooling rate adjustments to deliberately promote or suppress the development of short‐range ordering at grain boundaries
decision.why: Building on evidence that grain-boundary morphology (e.g., serration achieved via slower cooling) can redistribute strain and delay intergranular fracture, the next logical step is to test whether dynamic, service-condition thermal aging triggers a development of local chemical or ordering fluctuations at the boundaries. By varying cooling rates and aging times under conditions that mimic operational environments, one can compare specimens for signs of induced short-range ordering and concomitant toughness degradation. This controlled experiment directly distinguishes the proposed mechanism—dynamic grain-boundary short-range ordering—from conventional segregation/precipitation models.
